new_statements.quote: The relevant surface factors governing these stress patterns are the presence of an onset, the length of the first vowel, and the size of the root. The relevance of onsets is reflected in bisyllabic roots: roots starting with a short vowel like ikan have second-syllable stress, while roots starting with a consonant like katha have first-syllable stress. [...] The relevance of root size is reflected in the location of primary stress on the second syllable for all trisyllabic roots, regardless of onset or vowel length. [p. 10] [...] Right alignment immediately captures the fact that all patterns except the first one have stress on the penultimate syllable. [p. 12]
new_statements.citation: Verstraete, Jean-Christophe. 2021. Stress change and initial consonant loss in Umpithamu: Cause or consequence? Transactions of the Philological Society 119(2): 152-173. doi:10.1111/1467-968X.12210 (open author version, KU Leuven Lirias).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root in every root type except bisyllabic roots beginning with a short vowel (about 9% of roots), which are stressed on the final (second) syllable; so C-initial and long-vowel-initial bisyllables have initial stress, and all trisyllables have second-syllable stress. Verstraete formalises this as a right-aligned moraic trochee (long vowel = heavy; short onsetless initial = extra-light/unfooted), right-to-left parsing with a rightmost (primary) stress rule. Stress is not affected by suffixation. An alternative catalog coding would be fixed-penult with an onset/weight-conditioned exception class.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on a long-vowel initial syllable in trisyllabic roots (aaliman /ˌaːˈliman/, kaarrimpa /ˌkaːˈrimpa/); in compound-like quadrisyllables primary stress on the first element and secondary on the second (koorokooro /ˈkɔːɹɔˌkɔɹɔ/). Secondary stress is justified by metrical consistency and 'frequent misperception as primary stress in the author's initial fieldwork'.
new_statements.exceptions: Some C-initial bisyllabic roots ending in a lateral, especially approximant-initial ones, attract stress to the second syllable, mostly in free variation but fixed in a few (yayil /jaˈjil/, wukal /wuˈkal/); quadrisyllabic forms are diachronically complex (compounds or trisyllables with a historical increment) and reduce to the bisyllabic/trisyllabic patterns; a shortened variant iila of iilatha keeps second-syllable stress irregularly.
new_statements.domain_note: Root/word level: patterns listed for roots in lexical elicitation, where the word coincides with the utterance; diagnostic is the location of the primary pitch movement, backed by foot-conditioned plosive voicing. Stress is morphologically insensitive (unlike Yintyingka). Based on 755 roots in the Verstraete 2020 dictionary, from the late Florrie Bassani's speech.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language Umpithamu (also Uuku Umpithamu, Mumpithamu clan); Glottolog's name is Umbindhamu, umbi1243, ISO umd — same language (Middle Paman, Princess Charlotte Bay, Lamalama people). Data come from the last fluent speaker, the late Florrie Bassani, as documented in Verstraete 2020; no dialect distinction is made.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Word stress and stress shift' (author-version pp. 8-17) gives a full synchronic analysis based on the 755-root lexicon of Verstraete 2020: Table 3 lists eight root shapes; primary stress is penultimate in all except bisyllabic roots beginning with a short vowel (ikan /iˈkan/), which take final stress; C-initial and long-V-initial bisyllables have initial stress (katha /ˈkat̪a/, uuku /ˈuːku/); all trisyllables have second-syllable stress, with secondary stress on a long-vowel initial (aaliman /ˌaːˈliman/).
